::: {.callout-important}
### All code on this page is example code

UK Biobank studies differ widely in which variables are extracted, what
recoding makes sense, and what quality checks are relevant. Every example
here must be reviewed and adapted to your own study variables. The Field IDs,
category codes, and column names used are illustrations — yours will differ.
:::

This page walks through [`scripts/manage_dataset.R`](https://github.com/saras-clin/UKB_help/blob/main/scripts/manage_dataset.R),
which covers the steps between loading your raw extracted dataset and having
a clean, analysis-ready file.

- [Step 1: Inspect](#sec-inspect)
- [Step 2: Rename variables](#sec-rename)
- [Step 3: Convert variable types](#sec-types)
- [Step 4: Recode categoricals to factors](#sec-recode)
- [Step 5: Create derived variables](#sec-derived)
- [Step 6: Data quality checks](#sec-checks)

---

## Step 1: Inspect {#sec-inspect}

Before changing anything, run these to see exactly what you have:

```r
dplyr::glimpse(dataset)   # names, types, and sample values for every column
names(dataset)            # just the column names
sapply(dataset, class)    # type of each column as a named vector
```

UK Biobank column names follow a `p<FieldID>` format, with `_i0`, `_i1` etc.
for repeated measures (instances). For example:

| Column name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `p31` | Sex |
| `p34` | Year of birth |
| `p53_i0` | Date of baseline assessment (Instance 0) |
| `p53_i1` | Date of assessment (Instance 1) |
| `p191` | Date lost to follow-up |

Look up any Field ID on the [UK Biobank Data Showcase](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/).

---

## Step 2: Rename variables {#sec-rename}

UKB column names (`p31`, `p34_i0`, etc.) are not self-documenting. Renaming
them early makes every subsequent line of code easier to read and reduces
the risk of using the wrong column.

```r
rename_variables <- function(data) {
  renames <- c(
    sex                     = "p31",
    year_birth              = "p34",
    month_birth             = "p52",
    date_baseline           = "p53_i0",
    date_lost_to_followup   = "p191",
    current_tobacco_smoking = "p1239_i0",
    ethnicity               = "p21000_i0",
    physical_activity       = "p22032_i0"
  )
  renames_present <- renames[renames %in% names(data)]
  dplyr::rename(data, dplyr::all_of(renames_present))
}

dataset <- rename_variables(dataset)
```

The `renames_present` line filters to only columns that actually exist in
your dataset — this prevents errors if a field was not included in your
extraction.

---

## Step 3: Convert variable types {#sec-types}

After loading from parquet, check that each column has the correct R type.
Parquet usually preserves types well, but mismatches are common for dates
and IDs.

```r
convert_variable_types <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      eid = as.integer(eid),              # always integer for safe joins

      date_baseline         = as.Date(date_baseline),
      date_lost_to_followup = as.Date(date_lost_to_followup),

      year_birth  = as.integer(year_birth),
      month_birth = as.integer(month_birth)
    )
}

dataset <- convert_variable_types(dataset)
```

To check all types at once:

```r
sapply(dataset, class)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
### eid must always be integer

`eid` must be the same type in every table before joining. A mismatch between
integer and character eid silently produces zero rows with no error. Always
coerce to `as.integer(eid)` in every data frame before a join.
:::

---

## Step 4: Recode categorical variables to factors {#sec-recode}

UKB stores categorical variables as integers (e.g. Sex: 0 = Female, 1 = Male).
Converting to R factors with human-readable labels makes tables and plots
self-documenting and prevents accidental arithmetic on categorical data.

::: {.callout-note}
### UKB negative codes mean something specific

UK Biobank uses negative integers for special responses:

- **-1** = Do not know
- **-3** = Prefer not to answer
- **-7** = None of the above (some fields)

These are different from `NA` (not linked, or question not asked). Give them
explicit labels rather than collapsing them into "Unknown".
:::

```r
recode_variables <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::mutate(

      # Field 31: Sex
      sex_cat = factor(
        dplyr::case_when(
          sex == 0   ~ "Female",
          sex == 1   ~ "Male",
          is.na(sex) ~ NA_character_,
          TRUE       ~ "Unknown"
        ),
        levels = c("Female", "Male", "Unknown")
      ),

      # Field 1239: Current tobacco smoking
      current_tobacco_smoking_cat = factor(
        dplyr::case_when(
          current_tobacco_smoking ==  0  ~ "No",
          current_tobacco_smoking ==  1  ~ "Yes",
          current_tobacco_smoking == -3  ~ "Prefer not to answer",
          is.na(current_tobacco_smoking) ~ NA_character_,
          TRUE                           ~ "Unknown"
        ),
        levels = c("No", "Yes", "Prefer not to answer", "Unknown")
      ),

      # Field 21000: Ethnicity
      # UKB uses hierarchical codes — both parent (e.g. 1 = White) and
      # sub-codes (e.g. 1001 = British, 1002 = Irish) appear. Group both.
      ethnicity_group = factor(
        dplyr::case_when(
          ethnicity %in% c(1, 1001, 1002, 1003)       ~ "White",
          ethnicity %in% c(2, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004) ~ "Mixed",
          ethnicity %in% c(3, 3001, 3002, 3003, 3004) ~ "Asian",
          ethnicity %in% c(4, 4001, 4002, 4003)       ~ "Black",
          ethnicity %in% c(5, 5001)                   ~ "Chinese",
          ethnicity %in% c(6, 6001, 6002)             ~ "Other",
          is.na(ethnicity)                            ~ NA_character_,
          TRUE                                        ~ "Unknown / not coded"
        ),
        levels = c("White", "Mixed", "Asian", "Black", "Chinese", "Other",
                   "Unknown / not coded")
      ),

      # Field 22032: Physical activity
      physical_activity_cat = factor(
        dplyr::case_when(
          physical_activity == 0   ~ "Low",
          physical_activity == 1   ~ "Moderate",
          physical_activity == 2   ~ "High",
          is.na(physical_activity) ~ NA_character_,
          TRUE                     ~ "Unknown"
        ),
        levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Unknown")
      )
    )
}

dataset <- recode_variables(dataset)
```

### How `case_when()` works here

`case_when()` evaluates conditions in order and assigns the label from the
first match. The three parts of each line are:

```
condition  ~  "label"
```

The final `TRUE ~ "Unknown"` is a catch-all: any row that did not match any
earlier condition lands here. A large "Unknown" count usually means a code
appears in your data that is not in the `case_when()` blocks — check with:

```r
table(dataset$sex, useNA = "ifany")          # raw numeric codes
table(dataset$sex_cat, useNA = "ifany")      # after recoding
```

## Step 5: Create derived variables {#sec-derived}

Some variables useful for analysis are not in the raw UKB fields but can be
calculated from them.

### Age at baseline

UKB provides year and month of birth but not day (for participant privacy).
Using the 15th of the month is a common convention.

```r
create_derived_variables <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::mutate(

      # Approximate date of birth (day set to 15th — see note above)
      date_birth = as.Date(
        paste(year_birth, sprintf("%02d", month_birth), "15", sep = "-")
      ),

      # Age at baseline (decimal years)
      age_baseline = as.numeric(
        difftime(date_baseline, date_birth, units = "days")
      ) / 365.25,

      # Age group
      age_group = cut(
        age_baseline,
        breaks = c(39, 49, 59, 69, Inf),
        labels = c("40–49", "50–59", "60–69", "70+"),
        right  = TRUE
      )
    )
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
### UKB baseline recruitment

UK Biobank recruited participants aged 40–69 between 2006 and 2010. If your
calculated age at baseline falls outside this range for most participants,
check `year_birth` and `date_baseline` for parsing errors.
:::

---

## Step 6: Data quality checks {#sec-checks}

Run these before analysis. They catch problems that produce silent errors or
biased results.

### Duplicate eids

Each participant should appear exactly once in the main dataset. Duplicates
usually indicate a join in `setup.R` introduced extra rows — typically a
one-to-many join where the right-hand table had multiple rows per participant.

```r
n_dup <- sum(duplicated(dataset$eid))
if (n_dup > 0) {
  warning(n_dup, " duplicate eids — check joins in setup.R")
}
```

### Missingness summary

```r
missingness <- dataset |>
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(),
                                 ~ mean(is.na(.)))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::everything(),
                      names_to  = "variable",
                      values_to = "prop_missing") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(prop_missing))

print(missingness |> dplyr::filter(prop_missing > 0.10))
```

High missingness in core variables (sex, age, date_baseline) is unusual.
High missingness in optional fields (physical activity, dietary measures) is
common and expected in UKB — these questions were not asked at all instances.

### Implausible values

```r
# Age at baseline: UKB range is 40–69 at recruitment
range(dataset$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)

# Dates: should not be in the future
max(dataset$date_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)
```

### Factor distributions

Always check recoded factors immediately after recoding. Unexpected "Unknown"
values indicate codes in your data that your `case_when()` blocks do not cover.

```r
table(dataset$sex_cat, useNA = "ifany")
table(dataset$ethnicity_group, useNA = "ifany")
```
